lesson.title: Does a Straight Line Even Belong Here?
lesson.summary: The linearity condition checks, using a residual plot, whether a straight line is actually the right shape for the relationship before trusting any slope-based inference built on it.
lesson.body:
Every formula used in the last three chapters, the slope, its standard error, the t-statistic, the confidence interval, is built on the assumption that a straight line is actually the right shape for describing the relationship between x and y. If the true relationship curves, then fitting a straight line and reporting a slope for it is answering a question that doesn't really apply: the 'slope' of a line forced onto curved data doesn't have a stable, honest meaning, and it changes depending on which x-values happen to be in the sample.

The standard way to check this is not to stare at the original scatterplot, where mild curvature can be surprisingly easy to miss, but to look at a residual plot: the residuals (actual minus predicted) plotted against x, or against the predicted values. A good linear fit leaves residuals that look like random static, scattered above and below 0 with no leftover shape. A curved relationship squeezed into a straight line leaves a systematic pattern behind, typically a U-shape or an upside-down U, because the line over-predicts in some regions and under-predicts in others in a structured way.

Here's a deliberately extreme example to make the pattern unmistakable. Take x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, which is exactly y = x². Fitting a least-squares line anyway: mean x = 3, mean y = 11, and the slope comes out to b1 = 6 (from SSxy = 60 divided by SSxx = 10), with intercept b0 = 11 − 6(3) = −7. So the fitted line is predicted y = −7 + 6x. The residuals are: at x = 1, predicted −1, actual 1, residual 2; at x = 2, predicted 5, actual 4, residual −1; at x = 3, predicted 11, actual 9, residual −2; at x = 4, predicted 17, actual 16, residual −1; at x = 5, predicted 23, actual 25, residual 2. Lined up, those residuals read 2, −1, −2, −1, 2: a textbook U-shape, positive at both ends and most negative in the middle. That shape is the residual plot shouting that a straight line is the wrong model here, even though the least-squares line technically 'fits' in the sense of minimizing squared error.

Compare that to the six residuals from the hours-studied example in the last chapters: 0, 0.2, −0.6, 0.6, −0.2, 0. There's no consistent rise-then-fall or fall-then-rise, just small, unpatterned back-and-forth scatter, which is consistent with linearity holding reasonably well (with the honest caveat that six points is a small amount of evidence to judge shape from).

When linearity fails, the fix is not to run the t-test anyway and hope for the best, because a small p-value from a mis-specified model doesn't mean what it's supposed to mean. The usual next steps, transforming a variable or fitting a genuinely curved model, go beyond what this course covers, but recognizing the problem from a residual plot is the essential first move.
